All chess pieces have relative value. A pawn is 1, a knight or bishop are 3, a rook is 5 and a queen is 9. If you are a beginner your best strategy is to just try to make valuable trades. So if you can trade a knight for a rook, do it. Be sure too look out for the effects of your move a couple steps out. Like, if your bishop takes their rook but this allows them to take your knight without recourse then it is not a good trade.

I know it all has to do with mobility and how many spaces a piece can threaten in a given situation. Knights are really unique because they can jump pieces so in certain situations they are better than anything, but they are also very limited in their application and can't move across the board in a single move so that is why they aren't ranked higher. If you play a little bit you will notice that the rooks ability to move up down left or right makes it a lot more powerful than a bishop that can only move diagonally. A bishop that is on a white space can never be on a black space and vice versa, but a rook can occupy a white or a black space. As to why a bishop and knight are equal, I have no clue but I'm sure mathematicians have crunched the numbers and they are about equally valuable. Something that is also important to note is different pieces are better at different times in the game. Kinghts are definitely more effective early when the board is crowded and rooks don't really shine until later in the game when they have more freedom to move around.

Completely correct. Terms need definitions. But disagreeing over definitions is not productive. So when one does disagree there are essentially three possible productive responses:

  1. Argue that one definition does a better job of capturing some intuition shared by all parties (for obvious reasons this is very difficult).

  2. Use multiple definitions and keep track of them by some labeling schema. This allows one to say something like "This is censorship_devildetails but not censorship_otheruser."

  3. Taboo the problematic word completely and simply discuss the issue in terms of simpler words.

But insisting that one definition is correct or not is in not in general productive.

My answer is actually "No". I wouldn't. I would think that person is a fucking idiot, but I wouldn't write articles in a newspaper or magazine or on social media "calling them out" for being a racist. I wouldn't obsess over exacting my revenge, disguised as justice, on another human being. I wouldn't tell all his friends to have him socially ostracized. I'd say "That guy's a douche" move on with my life.
